fetched_contents.text: Response times in rural areas for emergency medical services, fire and rescue services and voluntary first responders during out-of-hospital cardiac arrests Abstract Aim To increase survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA), great efforts are made to improve the number of voluntary first responders (VFR). However, evidence of the potential utility of such efforts is sparse, especially in rural areas. Therefore, the aim was to describe and compare response times for emergency medical services (EMS), fire and rescue services (FRS), and VFR during OHCA in relation to population density. Methods This observational and comparative study was based on data including positions and time stamps for VFR and response times for EMS and FRS in a region in southern Sweden. Results In total, 285 OHCAs between 1 July 2020 and 31 December 2021 were analysed. VFR had the shortest median response time in comparison to EMS and FRS in all studied population densities. The overall median (Q1–Q3) time gain for VFR was 03:07 (01:39–05:41) minutes. A small proportion (19.2%) of alerted VFR accepted the assignments. This is most problematic in rural and sub-rural areas, where there were low numbers of alerted VFR. Also, FRS had shorter response time than EMS in all studied population densities except in urban areas. Conclusion The differences found in median response times between rural and urban areas are worrisome from an equality perspective. More focus should be placed on recruiting VFR, especially in rural areas since VFR can potentially contribute to saving more lives. Also, since FRS has a shorter response time than EMS in rural, sub-rural, and sub-urban areas, FRS should be dispatched more frequently. Keywords: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, Emergency medical services, Fire and rescue services, Voluntary first responders, Response times Introduction Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Annually, approximately 275,000 people suffer from OHCA treated by emergency medical services (EMS) in Europe, of which about 10% survive to hospital discharge.1, 2 Immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and early defibrillation are crucial in improving the chance of survival.3, 4 Therefore, shortening EMS response times in OHCA is important.5, 6, 7, 8 Availability goals for EMS response times differ between countries, where, for example, the UK has a predetermined goal for OHCA call response independent of whether it occurs in urban or rural areas — in average not exceeding 7 minutes, and responding to 90% within 15 minutes.9 Availability goals for EMS response times in Sweden differ considerably between regions.10 As in other countries,11 the most prolonged response times are seen for ambulance units stationed in rural areas.12. To shorten response time, great efforts have been made to involve fire and rescue service (FRS) as well as volunteer first responders (VFR). Consequently, FRS in most Swedish regions are dual-dispatched and/or dispatched to shorten the response time when it is assumed they will arrive before ambulance personnel to perform lifesaving interventions.13, 14, 15 FRS integrated into EMS as first responders contribute substantially to decreased OHCA response times, especially in rural areas.4, 6, 7 Also, implementing smartphone systems to alert VFR in case of OHCA increases the rate of early CPR and defibrillation and improves patient outcomes.16, 17 In some Nordic countries, VFR are most commonly alerted in urban OHCAs, resulting in shortened response times in comparison to EMS.18, 19, 20 However, although European guidelines strongly encourage the implementation of technology to alert VFR,21 such potential life-saving efforts have not been specifically evaluated in rural areas. Method Study design and setting This observational study was conducted in a region in southern Sweden over the course of 18 months between 1 July 2020 and 31 December 2021. The region has a population of 200,000 inhabitants and an area of 8,458 km2, which is divided into eight municipalities including two cities: one with approximately 71,000 inhabitants and one with 16,000 inhabitants. Overall population density is 24/km2 with a range between municipalities from 8.1 to 57.0 inhabitants/km2. Ethical approval was received from the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (No. 2021–00563). Emergency medical communication centre (EMCC) In 2020, the regional EMCC had an availability goal of answering emergency calls not exceeding a mean of 8 seconds, ≥92% within 15 seconds, and all calls in less than 30 seconds.22 In OHCA events, the EMCC dispatched two ambulances, and FRS were dispatched if only one ambulance was available or if FRS were assessed as being first on scene. The EMCC dispatcher determines the OHCA position according to the caller’s description or global positioning system (GPS) coordinates. ## Final integrated answer

### 1) What the physician’s advice means in practical terms

The physician’s advice is straightforward and urgent: if a newborn is **unresponsive and not breathing**, the first thing you should do is **call emergency services immediately** and then begin **infant CPR** if trained [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R2]. The evidence supports this as standard newborn emergency care: if a baby or child is unresponsive and not breathing normally, you should call 999 or the local emergency number and start CPR straight away [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The broader CPR guidance also says to check the scene, call the local emergency number, and provide care [N5-R1], and that if you are alone, you can give rescue breaths and chest compressions for one minute and then call 999 [N5-R4].

While waiting for help, the evidence emphasizes several actions: keep the baby’s airway clear, keep them warm, and continue CPR until help arrives or the baby starts breathing [N1-F1]. The infant CPR instructions in the evidence also specify the technique: use two fingers to push on the baby’s chest hard and fast 30 times, then give two breaths, and repeat until help arrives [N3-R5]. Another CPR source says to place the heel of one hand in the center of the child’s chest with the other hand on top, and to push down hard and fast about 2 inches at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute [N3-R1]. However, the evidence here is more consistent with **child CPR** than **infant CPR**, so it should be interpreted cautiously in this newborn context.

### 2) How regional emergency resources affect the response

Regional emergency resources **do vary by region**, and this directly affects response times and availability. The evidence shows that EMS response times differ considerably between regions in Sweden [N2-F2], and that availability goals for EMS response times differ between countries, with some regions having longer response times in rural areas [N2-F2]. Another study reports that response times in rural areas can take almost 20 minutes longer than the national average [N2-R2]. These findings support the conclusion that emergency service availability is not uniform and can be worse in some regions than in others.

The evidence also shows that response time differences can be significant enough to matter clinically. In southern Sweden, VFR had the shortest median response time in comparison to EMS and FRS in all studied population densities, and FRS had shorter response time than EMS in rural, sub-rural, and sub-urban areas [N2-F2]. This indicates that access to emergency help can depend not only on geography but also on the type of service dispatched. The CDC evidence further notes geographic disparities in EMS revenue, spending, and CVD quality indicators, and that EMS response times were 10% longer in lower-income neighborhoods [N6-R3]. The redlining study likewise shows structural disparities in rapid EMS access associated with historically redlined areas [N6-R1], and another study confirms spatial disparities in EMS provision across Busan [N6-R5]. Together, these sources show that regional access to emergency services can vary by geography, income, and social status.

### 3) The safest overall approach for the patient’s situation

The safest overall approach is to treat this as a **time-sensitive emergency** and follow the sequence:

#### Step 1: Call emergency services immediately
If the baby is unresponsive and not breathing, the first priority is to call emergency services immediately. The evidence and physician advice both say to contact emergency services first because every minute counts [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R2]. If someone else is present, have them make the call while you check the baby, so you can stay with the baby while help is summoned [N1-F1].

#### Step 2: Begin infant CPR if trained
If you are trained, begin infant CPR immediately [N1-F1]. The evidence supports starting CPR straight away if the baby is unresponsive and not breathing normally [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The recommended technique is to use two fingers to push on the baby’s chest hard and fast 30 times, then give two breaths, and repeat until help arrives [N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that child CPR guidance uses a different technique, placing the heel of one hand in the center of the child’s chest with the other hand on top and pushing down hard and fast about 2 inches at 100 to 120 per minute [N3-R1]. However, for a newborn, the newborn-specific CPR instructions in the evidence are more relevant than the child CPR wording.

#### Step 3: Keep the baby’s airway clear, keep them warm, and continue CPR
While waiting for help, make sure the baby’s airway is clear, keep them warm, and continue CPR until help arrives or the baby starts breathing [N1-F1]. The broader CPR guidance also says to keep the scene safe, shout for help, and then start CPR if alone [N5-R1]. In this newborn context, the evidence supports keeping the airway clear, keeping the baby warm, and continuing CPR [N1-F1].

#### Step 4: Prepare for possible delays or no immediate help
Because regional emergency resources vary by region, you should be prepared that help may take longer to arrive. The evidence shows that response times can be significantly longer in rural areas and in places with geographic, income, or structural disparities [N2-F2][N2-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5]. If no ambulance is immediately available, the evidence recommends continuing CPR and focusing on gentle compressions and rescue breaths as recommended for newborns [N1-F1]. It also supports trying to reach any available emergency service or nearby clinic while continuing CPR until the baby starts breathing or professional help arrives [N1-F1].

### 4) Practical takeaway for the patient

The patient’s question is essentially asking: **if the baby is not breathing, what should I do, and how does the region affect the answer?** The answer is that the region **does matter**, because emergency service availability and response times can vary widely by location [N2-F2][N2-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5]. But the core response should still be the same:

- **Call emergency services immediately**, because every minute counts [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R2].
- **If trained, begin infant CPR immediately** and continue until help arrives or the baby starts breathing [N1-F1][N3-R5].
- **If someone else is present, have them make the call while you check the baby** [N1-F1].
- **Keep the baby’s airway clear, keep them warm, and follow CPR instructions until help arrives** [N1-F1].
- **If no ambulance is immediately available, keep trying to reach emergency services or a nearby clinic and continue CPR** [N1-F1].

So, **yes, you should call emergency services** [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R2]. The physician’s advice is exactly what the evidence supports: immediate emergency calling first, then CPR if trained, while staying calm and following instructions from the emergency operator [N1-F1].

### 5) Bottom line

In short:  
- **Call emergency services immediately** [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R2].  
- **If trained, begin infant CPR immediately** [N1-F1][N3-R5].  
- **Keep the baby’s airway clear, keep them warm, and continue CPR until help arrives** [N1-F1].  
- **Regional differences can make help slower in some areas**, especially rural or low-income/disadvantaged regions [N2-F2][N2-R2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].  
- **If no ambulance is available nearby, keep trying to reach help and keep doing CPR** [N1-F1].

That is the safest overall approach for the patient’s situation.
